heading: Mystification & Mystery (Bentham, Marx, Carlyle)
source: Burke, Kenneth. A Rhetoric of Motives. University of California Press, 1950.
outline: Rhetorical Analysis in Bentham (pp.90-101): triplicate vocabulary, censorial appellative, covering motive, tegumen/res tegenda, rhetoric-in-spite-of-itself
Marx on 'Mystification' (pp.101-110): seven senses of ideology; inverted genealogy of culture; specific vs. generic motives; mystification as rhetorical diagnosis

Terministic Reservations in View of Cromwell's Motives (pp.110-114): context of situation qualifies Marxist critique; god-terms as implicit material counters; La Rochefoucauld on self-knowing conspiracy

Carlyle on 'Mystery' (pp.114-122): mystery as structural condition of hierarchic difference; class-erotic analogy; hierarchy as eulogistic bureaucracy; clothes-as-symbol doctrine; mystery equated with class distinctions

concepts.label: Mystery
concepts.gloss: The rhetorical condition arising where different kinds of beings communicate across a structural social divide. Requires both strangeness and the possibility of communion; generated by any pronounced social distinction — rank, class, age, race. Not subjective feeling but an objective structural effect of hierarchic difference.

concepts.label: Mystification
concepts.gloss: The rhetorical operation (Marx's dyslogistic term for mystery's social function) by which specific class interests are concealed beneath apparently universal or spiritual motive-terms. The ideological substitution of generic for specific that produces 'illusion' in Marx's technical sense.

concepts.label: Hierarchy
concepts.gloss: The eulogistic term for bureaucracy — a graduated social structure in which each rank employs a double rhetoric of deference upward and condescension downward, permeated by the spirit of the Ultimate Stage. Hierarchy is the scenic condition within which mystery operates.

concepts.label: Triplicate Vocabulary (Bentham)
concepts.gloss: Bentham's system: every domain of motive yields a neutral term flanked by eulogistic and dyslogistic counterparts. The neutral ideal is never a rhetorical reality — uninflected vocabulary cannot induce action. The eulogistic/dyslogistic poles are the normal condition of motivated discourse.

concepts.label: Censorial Appellative
concepts.gloss: Bentham's term for a word carrying evaluative weight as though descriptive — having the force of an assumption without its form. The tonal weight preloads the conclusion before the argument establishes it. Burke equates this with petitio principii as the normal operation of rhetorical discourse.

concepts.label: Covering Motive (tegumen / res tegenda)
concepts.gloss: When the actual motive behind an act cannot be presented eulogistically, a speaker selects the most favorable co-operative motive and presents it as the whole or essence. The linguistic veil (tegumen) over the interest concealed (res tegenda). Links Bentham's vocabulary analysis to Burke's theory of identification.

concepts.label: Ideology (Marxist technical sense)
concepts.gloss: The inverted genealogy of culture that treats ideas as causally primary when they are derivative of material (property and labor) conditions. In Burke's reconstruction of Marx, the seventh and most analytically significant sense of 'ideology' — the root mechanism of mystification.

concepts.label: Generic vs. Specific Motives
concepts.gloss: Burke's reconstruction of Marx's key distinction: generic motives appear universal ('humanity,' 'liberty'); specific motives are class-determined and material. Mystification is the rhetorical substitution of generic for specific — presenting the particular interest as universal truth.

concepts.label: Terministic Reservation
concepts.gloss: Burke's qualification of the Marxist diagnostic: terms carry implicit situational meanings users held tacitly; a term may appear far more idealized to later critics than to contemporaries who used it against a lived material context. Warns against reading mystification back into documents without recovering context of situation.

concepts.label: Via Negativa (secularized)
concepts.gloss: Burke detects behind Bentham's neutralization project a secularized mystical structure: withdrawal from weighted partisan language toward a neutral ground, followed by return with a new evaluative order. Eulogistic and dyslogistic 'change places' with neutral as the transitional stage. Anticipates treatment of mystery as categorical traversal.

concepts.label: Eulogistic / Dyslogistic
concepts.gloss: Bentham's paired terms for the evaluative poles of the censorial spectrum. Burke uses them throughout to track how the same act or condition is named for rhetorical advantage. Carlyle and Marx differ primarily in treating mystery eulogistically vs. dyslogistically; Burke refuses to adjudicate.

concepts.label: God-Term
concepts.gloss: A high-abstraction summarizing word — 'honor,' 'liberty,' 'Providence,' 'Absolute Idea' — gathering a complex of material conditions under a single spiritualized label. Cromwell's example shows god-terms are not necessarily mystifying to original users who recognize their material content. Anticipates the fuller treatment of Ultimate Terms in RM-05.

concepts.label: Identification via Mystery
concepts.gloss: Extends RM-01's substance-theoretic identification into the social axis: the clerk and manager are identified with and by different social principles. Mystery is the medium of differential identification — the felt awareness that communication crosses a categorical boundary, generating rhetorical charge from the crossing.

concepts.label: Rhetoric of Courtship (Class Analogue)
concepts.gloss: The formal analogy between erotic and inter-class rhetoric: relations between social ranks reproduce the full spectrum of courtship — appeal, seduction, coercion, submission, fascination. Not metaphor but structural homologue: both are rhetorics of crossing categorical boundaries. Prepares RM-06's full courtship analysis.

concepts.label: Symbol / Clothes (Carlyle)
concepts.gloss: Carlyle's clothes as symbols in general: visible emblems of social distinctions that simultaneously conceal common humanity and reveal hierarchic order as expression of a divine principle. Symbol carries doubled significance — concealment and revelation together. Connected forward to RM-07's treatment of the secret and pure persuasion.

concepts.label: Ultimate Identification (Hero-Worship)
concepts.gloss: Carlyle's doctrine of hero-worship as the 'identification' principle at the summit of hierarchy: the king summarizes all heroic figures; community identifies with the divine through identification with him. Connected to RM-07's ultimate identification and to the pentad's Agent term as the figure in whom hierarchy is personified.

concepts.label: Attitude as Tonal Gesture
concepts.gloss: The censorial appellative operates as an attitude — an incipient orientation that disposes without determining, shapes subsequent judgment without completing an argument. Headlines as postures/gestures (p.98). Reinforces the 6th dramatistic term seeded in the Grammar and picked up in Bentham's explicit discussion of 'incipient act' (p.91).

positions.claim: Bentham's attempt to expose the imagery concealed in abstract legal and moral vocabulary constitutes an accidental rhetoric — a systematic catalogue of persuasive technique produced in the service of would-be scientific neutrality.

A genuinely neutral vocabulary would defeat its own rhetorical ends: without evaluative charge, language cannot induce action. Neutralization is always partial, and the residual charge is always functional.

The Marxist analysis of rhetoric is primarily a contribution to the theory of Vague Generalities (Bentham): it discloses sinister factional interests concealed in bourgeois terms for benign universal interests, giving grand structural foundations to Bentham's notion of interest-begotten prejudice.

Mystery arises structurally wherever different kinds of beings are in communication: strangeness and the possibility of communion must coexist. Any pronounced social distinction — rank, class, age, race — sets the conditions for mystery.

Over and above all the qualifications, mystery is equated with class distinctions. Burke neither endorses nor debunks; he identifies the equivalence beneath both Carlyle's eulogistic and Marx's dyslogistic treatments.

Even the most mystifying of ultimate terms may subsume important materialistic content; and even the most apparently materialist ultimate vocabulary spiritualizes the pragmatic details of administration and governance. Neither Providence nor dialectical materialism escapes the mystifying function of high abstraction.

Hierarchy is the eulogistic word for bureaucracy, in which each stage employs a rhetoric of obeisance upward and condescension downward — a rhetoric of courtship throughout — while the Ultimate Stage is ideologically interpreted as the cause of the whole structure.

calleja_pim_candidates.rationale: Mystery as the rhetoric arising between beings of different social kinds maps to guild rank, prestige hierarchies, and elite player status in multiplayer games: different players represent different social principles, generating the fascination and deference Burke identifies as the phenomenology of mystery across hierarchic difference.

Mystification as the concealment of specific material system-logic behind apparently neutral or benign terms maps to hidden drop rates, opaque matchmaking, and undisclosed reward-probability structures — game-design instances of ideological motive-concealment in the Marxist technical sense.

Bentham's triplicate vocabulary maps to the moral naming of player choices in game narrative: the same in-game act is named neutrally, eulogistically, or dyslogistically depending on the game's ideological orientation, shaping the player's experience of moral weight and narrative meaning.

tensions.description: Bentham's project of vocabulary neutralization vs. the impossibility of neutral terms: the very aspiration to neutrality is a rhetorical stance, and the Benthamite neutral is a regulatory ideal that cannot function as rhetorical inducement without recovering some evaluative charge.

Marx's dyslogistic mystification vs. Carlyle's eulogistic mystery: both address the same social phenomenon (class hierarchy generating rhetorical difference), but where Marx sees concealment to be exposed, Carlyle sees revelation to be reverenced. Burke refuses to adjudicate, treating both as evaluative framings of the same structural condition.

The Marxist claim that ultimate terms (god-terms) are mystifying to those who use them vs. Burke's terministic reservation: users may tacitly carry the material content that the term summarizes, making it mystifying only to later critics who read the documentary residue without context of situation.

Bentham's ideal of a neutral vocabulary midway between eulogistic and dyslogistic extremes vs. Aristotle's model of virtue as the mean between two vicious extremes: in Bentham the neutral terms are themselves without moral weight; in Aristotle the middle terms are themselves eulogistic. No 'neutral' terms in Aristotle's sense.
